Scream 7

Kevin Williamson finally gets to direct the franchise he created three decades ago, and the result is a film that knows exactly what it wants to be emotionally ……

Film · Theatrical February 28, 2026 Analyzed by VirtueVigil Editorial Team 11 min read
Woke Score
12.46
Traditional Score
18.62

62%
Score Margin
+6 TRAD
Overall Perspective

Kevin Williamson finally gets to direct the franchise he created three decades ago, and the result is a film that knows exactly what it wants to be emotionally but cannot figure out how to get there structurally. Scream 7 opens this weekend to a franchise-record $59 million, making it the number one movie in America despite a 47% Rotten Tomatoes critics score and a boycott campaign that was trending on social media for months. The gap between the cultural conversation around this film and the actual content of the film is wider than anything in the franchise's history.

The plot: Sidney Prescott (Neve Campbell) has built a quiet life in the small town of Pine Grove with her husband Mark (Joel McHale) and teenage daughter Tatum (Isabel May, named after Sidney's murdered best friend from the original). When a new Ghostface killer emerges claiming to be Stu Macher, the original killer Sidney put down with a television set to the head in 1996, her carefully constructed peace is shattered. Tatum becomes the primary target. The opening sequence is the film's best work: a couple (Jimmy Tatro and Michelle Randolph) has booked a stay at the Macher House, now converted into an Airbnb-style true crime experience. It is gruesome, funny, and meta in exactly the way Scream should be. Tatro takes a knife to the head. Randolph is burned alive. The tone is set.

From there, the film shifts to Pine Grove and slows down considerably. Williamson clearly wants to build the mother-daughter relationship between Sidney and Tatum before the bloodbath begins, and these scenes work. Campbell has never been better in this role. She plays Sidney as a woman who has survived so much violence that she cannot stop scanning for threats, even in her own home. When Tatum's boyfriend Ben (Sam Rechner) climbs through her bedroom window, Sidney's reaction is not parental annoyance but genuine physiological terror. When Tatum borrows a blazer that Sidney happened to be wearing the night Billy Loomis held a gun to her head, Campbell plays the recognition with a physical flinch that says more than dialogue could. This is a performance built on three decades of character history, and it shows.

The kills are brutal. Mckenna Grace's Hannah is slammed into a wall on a theater harness and eviscerated, her intestines spilling onto the stage. Celeste O'Connor's Chloe is slid across a bar into shattered glass, a shard puncturing her throat. Asa Germann's Lucas has his head impaled on a beer tap, with beer flowing from his mouth. Sam Rechner's Ben is gutted in front of Tatum on the street. The body count hits ten, tying Scream 2 and Scream 3. Williamson is not shy about the violence, and the practical effects work is some of the best the franchise has produced.

The problems begin with the Ghostface reveal, which critics have rightly identified as the weakest in the franchise. Three killers: Jessica (Anna Camp), Sidney's seemingly friendly neighbor who was inspired by Sidney's memoir to murder her abusive husband and then became obsessively fixated on Sidney as a symbol; Marco (Ethan Embry), a psychiatric orderly and former Google employee who built the AI deepfake of Stu Macher; and Karl Gibbs (Mark Consuelos), a Stab-obsessed institution patient who is dispatched early. Jessica's motivation has potential but is underdeveloped. Marco's motivation is barely addressed. The AI deepfake conceit, where Marco uses his tech skills to create convincing video of Stu, then cycles through deepfakes of previous Ghostface killers (Laurie Metcalf's Nancy Loomis, Scott Foley's Roman Bridger, David Arquette's Dewey Riley), is the film's most ambitious idea and its most divisive. It works as meta-commentary on nostalgia culture and the AI-driven resurrection of the dead. It does not work as a satisfying mystery resolution.

The film's meta-commentary on AI and toxic nostalgia is timely but shallow. Mindy (Jasmin Savoy Brown) delivers the obligatory rules monologue, this time about how legacy sequels keep resurrecting what should stay dead. There is a scene where the Stu deepfake interacts with Gale Weathers that multiple critics have interpreted as a sly dig at Spyglass for firing Melissa Barrera. If intentional, it is the kind of self-aware provocation the franchise does well. If not, it is an extraordinary coincidence.

The Barrera situation is the elephant in every room this film walks through. Melissa Barrera was fired from Scream 7 in November 2023 after sharing pro-Palestine social media posts that Spyglass Media deemed antisemitic. Jenna Ortega, who played Barrera's on-screen sister Tara, initially cited scheduling conflicts with Netflix's Wednesday but later confirmed to The Cut that she left because of the Barrera situation and the production falling apart. The original directors Tyler Gillett and Matt Bettinelli-Olpin also departed. The entire Sam and Tara Carpenter storyline from Scream (2022) and Scream VI was abandoned, requiring a $500,000 rewrite that pivoted the story back to Sidney. Neve Campbell, who had publicly criticized her lowball salary offer for Scream VI, was brought back with significantly improved terms.

None of this backstage chaos is visible in the final product in any direct way, but its effects are everywhere. The film feels like two movies awkwardly stitched together: a genuine, emotionally grounded Sidney Prescott story (Williamson's vision) bolted onto a convoluted triple-killer mystery with an AI gimmick (the rewrite scaffolding). The seams show. The pacing sags in the middle. Characters who should matter, like Mark Consuelos's sheriff, feel like afterthoughts. Chad and Mindy show up halfway through and inject energy, but they are not given enough to do.

For the VirtueVigil audience, the ideological read is straightforward. Scream 7 is a surprisingly traditional film wrapped in the franchise's standard meta-progressive packaging. The emotional engine is a mother defending her daughter. The nuclear family is presented as worth fighting for. Sidney's husband Mark is supportive and competent without being emasculated. The killers' motivation is explicitly about twisted fandom and obsession, not systemic critique. The meta-commentary on AI and nostalgia is culturally relevant but not politically pointed. Mindy is queer-coded as always, but this is legacy franchise DNA, not new insertion. The biggest progressive element is arguably the film's implicit commentary on itself: a franchise that fired a Latina actress for political speech and brought back the white original lead, then made a movie about how nostalgia for the past can be weaponized. Whether that irony is intentional or accidental is the most interesting question Scream 7 raises, and it is a question the film has no interest in answering.

The audience clearly does not care about any of this. $59 million opening weekend. 74% audience score. The boycott was a cultural event that failed as an economic one. Scream 7 is the number one movie in America because enough people wanted to see Sidney Prescott come back and stab Ghostface in the face. On that specific promise, the film delivers.

Adult Viewer Insight

Conservative adults will find more to like here than in the previous two Scream entries. The core story is a mother fighting to protect her daughter from a serial killer. Sidney and Mark's marriage is presented as a genuine partnership. The nuclear family is the thing worth defending. The meta-commentary is present but lighter than Scream VI. Mindy's queer identity is background texture, not a sermon. The biggest potential irritant is the AI deepfake plot device, which some viewers will find gimmicky rather than clever. The violence is extreme and sustained. The killer reveal is weak. But the emotional sincerity of Campbell's performance anchors the whole thing. If you can tolerate franchise horror and do not need your entertainment to be explicitly conservative, Scream 7 will not offend you. It will just disappoint you slightly with its third act.

Parental Guidance

Rated R. Recommended minimum age: 16, ideally 17+. The violence in Scream 7 is graphic, sustained, and creative in ways designed to shock. Specific content parents should know about: a character is burned alive in the opening scene; a teenage girl is eviscerated on stage with her intestines visible; a character has his head impaled on a beer tap; a character is gutted in the street; multiple characters are stabbed repeatedly; one killer is shot approximately fifteen times in the head. There is mild sexual content (a boyfriend climbing through a bedroom window, some flirtation). Language is strong throughout. The film's themes of parental trauma, obsessive fandom, and AI-generated deception of the dead are worth discussing with mature teens who can handle the violence. Younger viewers should not see this film under any circumstances.
